tagline: A 1918 scenic highway links Front Range views and former mining towns
intro: Peak to Peak follows the Front Range with views of the Continental Divide and its forested approaches. The Colorado Department of Transportation presents it as a drive combining recreation and nature preservation, with national forests, Rocky Mountain National Park and Indian Peaks Wilderness among its attractions. CDOT lists 55 miles and 80 minutes of driving.

Established in 1918, it is Colorado’s oldest scenic byway. The route holds both National Forest Scenic Byway and Colorado Scenic and Historic Byway designations. Its numbered highways have their own history: the section north of Nederland was once SH 160, and SH 72 took over the Nederland-to-Raymond route in 1968.

Tourism was changing Allenspark during the same era: farmers and miners found better summer incomes serving visitors. The village grew as summer residents bought land and built cabins from around 1900 to 1920. Improved roads and modern technology later made year-round mountain living easier.

At Estes Park, Peak to Peak connects with Trail Ridge Road. Head south on SH 7 to Allenspark, then follow SH 72 past Ward to Nederland. SH 119 continues through Rollinsville toward Black Hawk, passing above South Boulder Creek at Rollinsville. Gravel roads branching from the highway lead to high-country lakes, trailheads, the Moffat Tunnel’s east portal and the ghost towns of Hesse and Apex.

moments.title: Chapel on the Rock
moments.text: The rock came before the chapel, and keeping it intact became part of the building’s story. Monsignor Joseph Bosetti encountered the formation in 1916 and envisioned a church on it. Lack of funds delayed construction for nearly 20 years, while Bosetti also struggled with the Colorado Highway Department to preserve the rock. Mr. and Mrs. Oscar Malo donated the land, and architect Jacques Benedict designed the chapel, completed in 1936. The chapel survived both the retreat center’s 2011 fire and the floods of 2013. Officially named Saint Catherine of Siena Chapel, it remains a functioning Catholic chapel on the Saint Malo grounds.

moments.title: Ward
moments.text: Ward’s schoolhouse helped defend the town during its January 1900 fire. Draped in wet blankets, it served as a firebreak for houses above while the lower town burned. Ward began in 1860 after gold was discovered at nearby Gold Hill; its mountainside site stands at 9,450 feet. The school had been built in 1898, the same year the railroad reached this mining community at the top of Left Hand Canyon. Profitable mines supported the town’s immediate rebuilding after the fire. The surviving school building later served as town hall, public library and post office.

moments.title: Nederland
moments.text: Nederland’s name describes its position below the mines that sent ore here for milling. The settlement had been called Dayton and Browns Crossing before the post office adopted Middle Boulder in 1871. Two years later, a company from the Netherlands bought the Caribou Mine. Wind and deep winter snow at the mine encouraged its owners to bring ore downhill to Middle Boulder. Dutch miners called the place Nederland, meaning low land; the town adopted that name when it incorporated in 1874. The modern highway junction is here too: SH 72 and SH 119 meet in town along the Peak to Peak route.
